157: There can be no doubt that nothing in this world is so indispensable as love.
I see that Charlotte could not lose me without a pang, and the children have only one wish — that I should come and visit them again tomorrow.
I went this afternoon to tune Charlotte's piano.
But I could not manage it, because the little ones insisted on my telling them a story, and Charlotte herself urged me to satisfy them.
I waited on them at tea, and they are now as fully contented with me as with Charlotte; and I told them my very best tale, of the princess who was waited on by dwarfs.
I improve by the exercise, and I am quite surprised at the impression my stories make.
If I sometimes invent an incident and then forget it the next time, they tell me at once that the story was different before.
So I now try to relate the same anecdote exactly, in the same unchanging tone.
From this I see how much an author injures his work by altering it, even when the change is an improvement in a poetical sense.
The first impression is readily received.
We are so made that we believe the most incredible things; and once they are engraved on the memory, woe to the man who tries to rub them out.
159: Must it always be so — that the source of our happiness must also be the fountain of our misery?

The full, ardent feeling that once animated my heart with the love of nature, overwhelming me with a torrent of delight and bringing all paradise before me, has now become an unbearable torment, a demon that pursues and harasses me everywhere.
In days gone by I would gaze from these rocks at the mountains across the river, and at the green, flowering valley below me, and see all nature budding and breaking open around me.
The hills were clothed from foot to summit with tall, thick forest trees.
The valleys in all their windings were shaded with the loveliest woods.
And the soft river slid along among the whispering reeds, mirroring the beautiful clouds that the evening breeze carried across the sky.
I heard the groves around me full of birdsong, and saw the million swarms of insects dancing in the last golden beams of the sun, whose setting rays woke the humming beetles out of their grassy beds.
The subdued stir all around turned my attention to the ground, where I saw the arid rock forced to yield nourishment to the dry moss, and the heath flourishing on the barren sands below me.
All of it showed me the inner warmth that animates the whole of nature, and it filled my heart and glowed there.
I felt myself raised by this overflowing fullness to a perception of the Godhead, and the glorious forms of an infinite universe became visible to my soul.
Stupendous mountains encircled me, abysses yawned at my feet, and cataracts fell headlong before me.
Impetuous rivers rolled across the plain, and rocks and mountains echoed from far off.
In the depths of the earth I saw innumerable powers in motion, multiplying to infinity; while on its surface, and under the heavens, ten thousand kinds of living creatures teemed.
Everything around is alive with an infinite number of forms, while mankind flies for safety into its petty houses, and from that shelter rules in imagination over the whole wide universe.
Poor fool, in whose small reckoning all things are small.

From the inaccessible mountains, across the desert no mortal foot has trodden, out to the edge of the unknown ocean, breathes the spirit of the eternal Creator; and every atom he has given existence to finds favour in his sight.
Ah, how often in those days the flight of a bird overhead filled me with the longing to be carried to the shores of the immeasurable waters.
To drink the pleasures of life there from the foaming goblet of the Infinite.
And to share, if only for a moment, with the confined powers of my soul, the blessedness of that Creator who accomplishes all things in himself and through himself.
160: My dear friend, the bare recollection of those hours still consoles me.
Even this effort to recall those unspeakable sensations and put them into words raises my soul above itself, and makes me feel doubly the intensity of my present anguish.
161: It is as though a curtain had been drawn back from my eyes, and instead of the prospect of eternal life, the abyss of an ever-open grave yawned in front of me.

Can we say of anything that it exists, when everything passes away — when time, with the speed of a storm, carries all things onward, and our brief existence, swept along by the torrent, is either swallowed by the waves or dashed against the rocks?
There is not a moment that does not prey upon you and on everything around you; not a moment in which you do not yourself become a destroyer.
The most innocent walk takes the lives of thousands of poor insects; one step wrecks the fabric of the industrious ant and turns a little world into chaos.
No: it is not the great and rare calamities of the world that move me — not the floods that sweep away whole villages, nor the earthquakes that swallow our towns.
My heart is wasted by the thought of that destructive power hidden in every part of universal nature.
Nature has formed nothing that does not consume itself and everything near it.
So, surrounded by earth and air and all the active powers, I go my way with an aching heart; and the universe is to me a fearful monster, for ever devouring its own offspring.
163: In vain I stretch out my arms toward her when I wake in the morning from my weary sleep.
In vain I feel for her at night in my bed, when some innocent dream has happily deceived me and set her beside me in the fields, and I have seized her hand and covered it with countless kisses.

And when I reach for her in the half confusion of sleep, in the happy certainty that she is near, tears flow from my oppressed heart, and, robbed of all comfort, I weep over the sorrows still to come.
165: My active spirits have sunk into a contented indolence.
I cannot be idle, and yet I am unable to set to work.
I cannot think; I have no feeling left for the beauties of nature, and books are distasteful to me.
Once we give ourselves up, we are lost entirely.
Many a time I wish I were a common labourer, so that on waking in the morning I might have one prospect, one pursuit, one hope for the day ahead.
I often envy Albert when I see him buried in a heap of papers and parchments, and fancy I should be happy in his place.
More than once, under that feeling, I have been on the point of writing to you and to the minister about the post at the embassy which you think I might obtain.
I believe I could get it.
The minister has long shown a regard for me, and has often urged me to look for employment.
It would be the business of an hour.
Now and then the fable of the horse comes back to me.
Weary of his liberty, he let himself be saddled and bridled, and was ridden to death for his pains.
I do not know what to decide.
For is not this longing for change just the restless spirit that would follow me into any situation in life?
167: If my troubles admitted of any cure, they would certainly be cured here.
This is my birthday, and early in the morning I received a packet from Albert.
On opening it I found one of the pink ribbons Charlotte wore in her dress the first time I saw her, and which I had several times asked her to give me.
With it were two small volumes of Wetstein's "Homer," a book I had often wished for, to save me the trouble of carrying the large Ernestine edition on my walks.
You see how they anticipate my wishes, how well they understand those small attentions of friendship, so far above the costly presents of the great, which only humiliate.
I kissed the ribbon a thousand times, and with every breath drew in the memory of those happy and irrecoverable days that filled me with the keenest joy.
I do not complain of it: the flowers of life are only apparitions.
How many pass away and leave no trace behind — how few yield any fruit — and the fruit itself, how rarely does it ripen!
And yet there are flowers enough; and is it not strange, my friend, that we should let the little that does ripen rot and perish unenjoyed?
I often climb into the trees in Charlotte's orchard and shake down the pears that hang on the highest branches.
She stands below and catches them as they fall.
169: Why do I deceive myself like this?
What is to come of all this wild, aimless, endless passion?
I can pray to no one but her.
My imagination sees nothing but her; everything around me counts for nothing except as it relates to her.
In this dreaming state I enjoy many happy hours, until at last I feel forced to tear myself away from her.
Ah, Wilhelm, what does my heart not drive me to!
When I have spent several hours in her company, until I am completely absorbed by her figure, her grace, the divine expression of her thoughts, my mind works itself up to the highest pitch.
My sight grows dim, my hearing confused, my breathing tightens as though a murderer's hand were on my throat, and my beating heart tries to find relief for my aching senses.
Sometimes I do not know whether I really exist.
If at such moments I find no sympathy, and Charlotte will not let me have the melancholy consolation of bathing her hand with my tears, I have to tear myself away from her.
Then I wander through the country, climb some steep cliff, or force a path through the trackless thicket, where the thorns and briers tear me — and there I find relief.
Sometimes I lie stretched on the ground, worn out with fatigue and dying of thirst.
Sometimes, late in the night, with the moon above me, I lean against an old tree in some remote forest to rest my weary limbs, and, exhausted, sleep there till daybreak.
O Wilhelm, the hermit's cell, his sackcloth and his girdle of thorns would be luxury and indulgence beside what I suffer.
I see no end to this wretchedness but the grave.
171: Thank you, Wilhelm, for settling my wavering purpose.
For a whole fortnight I have been thinking of leaving her.
She has gone back to town, and is staying at a friend's house.
And then there is Albert — yes, I must go.
173: After this I can bear anything.
I shall never see her again.
Oh, why can I not fall on your neck and pour out, in floods of tears and raptures, all the passions that tear at my heart!
Here I sit gasping for breath, struggling to compose myself.
I am waiting for daylight; at sunrise the horses are to be at the door.
174: And she is sleeping calmly, never suspecting that she has seen me for the last time.
I had the courage, through two hours of conversation, not to betray my intention.
And O Wilhelm, what a conversation it was!
175: Albert had promised to join Charlotte in the garden immediately after supper.
I was on the terrace under the tall chestnut trees, watching the setting sun.
I saw him sink for the last time below this lovely valley and its silent stream.
I had often stood on that spot with Charlotte and watched that glorious sight; and now I was walking up and down the very avenue that was so dear to me.

A secret sympathy had often drawn me there before I ever knew Charlotte; and we were delighted, early in our acquaintance, to discover that we both loved the same spot, which is as romantic as any that ever caught an artist's fancy.
176: From beneath the chestnut trees there is a wide view.

But I remember I have described all this in an earlier letter — the tall mass of beech trees at the end, and how the avenue grows darker and darker as it winds among them, until it ends in a gloomy recess that has all the charm of a mysterious solitude.
I still remember the strange melancholy that came over me the first time I stepped into that dark retreat, at bright midday.
I had some secret foreboding that it would one day be the scene of great happiness or great misery for me.
177: I had spent half an hour torn between the thought of going and the thought of staying, when I heard them coming up the terrace.
I trembled as I took her hand and kissed it.
As we reached the top of the terrace, the moon rose from behind the wooded hill.
We talked of many things, and without noticing it came to the gloomy recess.
Charlotte went in and sat down.
I did the same, but my agitation would not let me sit for long.
I got up and stood in front of her, then walked back and forth, then sat down again.
Charlotte drew our attention to the beautiful effect of the moonlight, which threw a silver hue over the terrace in front of us, beyond the beech trees.
It was a glorious sight, made more striking by the darkness that surrounded the spot where we sat.

We were silent for a while, and then Charlotte said, "Whenever I walk by moonlight, it brings back to me all my beloved and departed friends, and I am filled with thoughts of death and of what is to come."
"We shall live again, Werther!" she went on, in a firm but feeling voice. "But shall we know one another again? What do you think? What do you say?"
178: "Charlotte," I said, taking her hand in mine, my eyes filling with tears, "we shall see each other again — here and hereafter we shall meet again."
Why, Wilhelm, should she put that question to me, just at the moment when the fear of our cruel separation filled my heart?
179: "And oh, do those who have gone know how we spend our time here? Do they know when we are well and happy? Do they know when we call up their memory with the fondest love?"
"In the silent hour of evening the shade of my mother hovers around me."

"When I sit among my children and see them gathered near me as they used to gather near her, I raise my anxious eyes to heaven and wish she could look down on us, and see how I keep the promise I made her in her last moments, to be a mother to her children."
"With what feeling I then cry out: 'Pardon me, dearest of mothers, pardon me if I do not fill your place as I should!'"
"They are clothed and fed; and, better still, they are loved and brought up."
"Could you but see, sweet saint, the peace and harmony we live in, you would glorify God with the warmest gratitude — the God to whom, in your last hour, you prayed so fervently for our happiness.'"
So she spoke; but O Wilhelm, who can do justice to her words?
How can cold and passionless language convey the heavenly expression of a spirit?
"This affects you too deeply, my dear Charlotte. I know your soul dwells on such recollections with intense delight; but I beg you —"
"O Albert," she went on, "I am sure you have not forgotten the evenings when the three of us used to sit at the little round table, when papa was away and the little ones had gone to bed."
"You often had a good book with you, but you seldom read it; the conversation of that noble creature was better than anything — that beautiful, bright, gentle, and yet ever-toiling woman."
"God alone knows how often I have begged with tears on my bed at night that I might be like her."
180: I threw myself at her feet, seized her hand, and wet it with a thousand tears.
"Charlotte!" I exclaimed. "God's blessing and your mother's spirit are upon you."
"Oh, that you had known her," she said, pressing my hand warmly.
"She was worthy of being known to you."
I thought I should faint; never had I been given praise so flattering.
She went on: "And yet she was doomed to die in the flower of her youth, when her youngest child was barely six months old."
"Her illness was short, but she was calm and resigned; it was only for her children, and above all the youngest, that she was unhappy."
"When her end drew near, she told me to bring them to her."
"The younger ones knew nothing of what was coming, while the elder ones were quite overcome with grief."
"They stood around the bed, and she raised her feeble hands to heaven and prayed over them; then, kissing each in turn, she sent them away and said to me, 'Be a mother to them.'"
"I gave her my hand. 'You are promising a great deal, my child,' she said, 'a mother's fondness and a mother's care!'"

"'I have often seen, by your tears of gratitude, that you know what a mother's tenderness is. Show it to your brothers and sisters; and be as dutiful and faithful to your father as a wife would be. You will be his comfort.'"
"She asked for him. He had gone out to hide his unbearable anguish; he was heartbroken. 'Albert, you were in the room.'"
"She heard someone moving, asked who it was, and called you over."
"She looked at us both with an expression of composure and satisfaction, as if certain that we should be happy — happy with one another."
Albert fell on her neck and kissed her, and cried, "We are, and we shall be!"
Even Albert, usually so tranquil, had quite lost his composure; and I was moved beyond words.
181: "And such a being," she went on, "had to leave us, Werther!"
"Great God, must we part like this with everything we hold dear in this world?"
"Nobody felt it more keenly than the children: they cried and lamented for a long time afterwards, complaining that men had carried away their dear mamma."
182: It roused me; but I stayed sitting and held her hand.
"Let us go," she said. "It is growing late."
She tried to draw her hand away; I held it still.
"We shall see each other again," I cried. "We shall know each other through any change!"
"I am going," I went on, "going willingly; but if I said for ever, perhaps I should not keep my word."
"Yes — tomorrow, I think," she answered with a smile.
Tomorrow! How I felt that word.
Ah, she little knew, as she drew her hand away from mine.
I stood gazing after them in the moonlight.
I threw myself on the ground and wept; then sprang up and ran out onto the terrace, and saw, in the shade of the linden-trees, her white dress disappearing near the garden gate.
I stretched out my arms, and she was gone.
